paper_title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [2, 6, 7, 13, 25, 45] are rapidly evolving from static input processors into interactive agents that can operate in digital and physical environments. In particular, vision-language-action (VLA) models [24, 28, 46, 58] offer promising path toward embodied artificial general intelligence. However, high trial-and-error costs and the lack of environmental controllability significantly hinder both the evaluation and algorithm scaling of real-world physical agents. Modern large-scale games [4, 11, 32, 47, 5961] provide an ideal testbed for developing generalist VLA agents and studying their scaling behaviors because they combine realistic complexity with rigorous experimental control. Compared with traditional 2D games, web interfaces, and simplified simulators, contemporary games require agents to parse complex visual scenes, navigate intricate 3D layouts, and advance multi-stage quests. 1 Figure 1 Overview of Gamer. generalist game agent framework operates across broad range of visually and mechanically diverse games. At each step, the agent uses the current screen, task context, recent interaction history, long-term memory, and reasoning to generate native keyboard and mouse actions in real time. The agent interacts continuously through this loop. Cross-game training, multi-level supervision, and persistent memory support transferable control and sustained task execution. Agents must continually make strategic decisions and manage resources under partial observability and delayed feedback, all through fine-grained, low-level keyboard and mouse actions. Tasks may last hours or longer, requiring reliable memory, planning, and decision-making throughout. Such environments therefore serve as an uncompromising benchmark for coordinating perception, reasoning, memory, and control. Honkai: Star Rail (HSR) exemplifies this setting by condensing these demands into continuously evolving game environment. Its gameplay combines narrative-driven exploration across diverse regions with turn-based combat, squad management, resource allocation, and multi-level UI operation. This environment features nested objectives and long-term progression that challenge an agents cross-task generalization, long-term memory, and closed-loop execution. Developing agents in this system compels MLLMs to transition from passive visual understanding to sustained, proactive interaction. Mastering such challenges paves concrete pathway toward generalist agents capable of operating across both complex digital worlds and embodied physical environments. As illustrated in Figure 1, Gamer is designed to operate across visually and mechanically diverse environments via single screen-to-action interface. Although games have long served as standard testbeds for AI, extending these successes to modern, complex games remains challenging. With domain-specific policy optimization, prior agents have matched or exceeded human performance in benchmarks such as Atari [27], Minecraft [11], and StarCraft [43]. However, these methods typically use privileged internal states, tailored action spaces, or dedicated APIs, which generalize poorly beyond their narrow training domains. As summarized in Table 1, existing game agents differ substantially in their training recipes, game coverage, and real-time execution capabilities. Because modern games rarely expose internal states or dedicated interaction APIs, true generalist agent should operate like human player [33, 41, 51]: perceiving the world through raw visual pixels and acting through standard keyboard-and-mouse interfaces. Unifying transferable control, long-horizon decision-making, and non-invasive execution within single generalist model remains largely unaddressed. Unlike static benchmarks, dynamic game environments evolve continuously while an agent observes, reasons, and acts. Therefore, real-time interaction introduces critical system bottleneck. Here, BC, SFT, CPT, and RL denote behavior cloning, supervised fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning, respectively. We open-source our inference engine and checkpoints for CPT scaling behaviors. changed. Over long trajectories, these delays can lead to control errors, unnecessary interactions, and early failures. This latency penalty also affects online reinforcement learning (RL): delayed rollouts not only inflate wall-clock collection times but also dilute the quality of policy feedback. Consequently, real-time inference is not merely deployment requirement, but an important part of effective online learning. To address these challenges, we present Gamer, scalable generalist agent framework for complex interactive games. Gamer observes raw screen pixels and executes native keyboard and mouse controls. This unified device-level interface enables non-invasive interaction across diverse environments, eliminating reliance on game-specific APIs or customized action spaces. We first conduct continued pre-training (CPT) on thousands of hours of multi-source gameplay trajectories and map heterogeneous control formats into unified keyboardand-mouse representation to establish transferable control prior. scalable data-construction pipeline is built to transform raw gameplay trajectories into multi-level instruction data. Using LLM-assisted annotation, the pipeline adds task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and memory summaries while preserving the original observation-action sequences. We produce over thousand hours of instruction data covering local operations, intermediate subgoals, and complete tasks. We leverage this corpus for sparse-thinking instruction tuning, enabling the policy to organize executable behavior around long-horizon objectives while retaining task-relevant memory. Finally, we introduce Temporal-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (TA-GRPO) to further optimize the game policy through online environment feedback and address accumulated execution errors and sparse rewards over extended interactions. We support large-scale training and real-time deployment through unified training, evaluation, and inference infrastructure. We extend Verl [40] to support CPT, SFT, and online RL within shared training framework, with self-developed Streaming-vLLM serving as the inference engine for interactive evaluation and rollout generation. Streaming-vLLM combines stateful KV-cache reuse, architecture-aware execution, FSM-guided speculative decoding with BF16 verification, and streaming action dispatch to reduce inference latency. Equipped with sandbox supporting concurrent game instances and data pipeline that collects trajectories and identifies failures, this system enables iterative policy improvement under real-time interaction constraints. Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on several challenging 3D game tasks and achieves competitive performance on range of traditional 2D game benchmarks in real-time. These results demonstrate that unified keyboard-and-mouse action space which is coupled with cross-domain trajectory scaling and real-time online learning can offer viable pathway toward generalist interactive agents. We make the following contributions: generalist agent framework for complex games. Gamer interacts with complex game environments non-invasively, using screen images as input and standard keyboard and mouse operations as unified action space. We demonstrate how learning in this shared action space generalizes across diverse game. scalable pipeline for long-horizon instruction data construction. We develop pipeline that transforms multi-source and multi-format gameplay trajectories into instruction data. Through LLM-assisted 3 annotation and quality validation, the pipeline enriches recorded interactions with task instructions, reasoning at critical decisions, and persistent memory summaries. Applied to tens of thousands of hours of gameplay data, it produces over thousand hours of high-quality instruction data spanning operations, subgoals, and complete quests, providing supervision for long-horizon reasoning and control. Stable and scalable training, evaluation, and real-time inference. We extend Verl into unified training and evaluation framework spanning CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO and introduce Streaming-vLLM to support efficient online rollouts and deployment. Our RL approach optimizes memory-linked trajectory segments using verifiable environment feedback at scale. Strong empirical results. Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled human players on challenging 3D commercial game tasks, and achieves competitive performance on several traditional 2D game benchmarks. These results support its potential for industrial-scale deployment.

sections.title: 2 Continued Pre-Training for Cross-Game Control
sections.content: Games differ in world, mechanics, and objectives, but most games share unified device-level interface: screen observations and native keyboard and mouse inputs. As shown in Figure 2, CPT adapts pretrained multimodal model to this interface and learns transferable control from trajectories collected across environments. We first unify action representations across games and reduce biases caused by key frequencies and repeated control states. We then summarize findings from GameScaling [58] on how model capacity, gameplay data, and game composition affect control learning and cross-game generalization. Figure 2 CPT for unified keyboard-mouse control. Synchronized gameplay observations and device events are mapped to shared action representation. Random key remapping reduces reliance on key identity, while repeat-aware loss decay reweights temporally persistent actions. The resulting control prior is used by the subsequent task-conditioned training stages.

sections.title: 2.3 Scaling Laws and Cross-Game Generalization
sections.content: Although shared control interface makes cross-game CPT possible, the benefits of additional gameplay data depend on how well the training data cover the target environment. GameScaling [58] examines this dependence by varying model size, gameplay budget, and game composition. We summarize its findings here to contextualize Gamers CPT stage. To characterize these effects, composition-aware scaling relation based on D-CPT Law [35] is adopted. Let be model size, the gameplay budget in hours, and [0, 1] the proportion of gameplay relevant to specified validation distribution. The validation loss is modeled as Lval(N, D, q) = + CN + CDqη Db + Cq (q + ϵ)c , (6) where E, CN , CD, Cq, a, b, c, and η are fitted variables. The small constant ϵ > 0 keeps the expression finite when the target games share is zero. In view of the widespread use of Minecraft in prior work [11, 51], Gamescaling [58] varies its proportion in the gameplay mixture to study the effect of data composition. We use = wMC for Minecraft validation and = 1 wMC for validation over the remaining training-game distribution, where wMC is the Minecraft fraction of the gameplay mixture. The data term describes how validation loss changes with the gameplay budget, and the final term captures differences between data mixtures. The scaling relation fits the training-game distributions and supports held-out prediction within the measured range. However, distant unseen games do not exhibit sustained gains from additional CPT data. Sec. 8.2 provides the controlled study and its empirical limits. CPT thus provides transferable control, while more distant worlds and longer tasks motivate additional task-conditioned supervision and online interaction.

sections.title: 3 Supervised Fine-Tuning for Sparse Reasoning and Cross-Context Memory
sections.content: CPT learns transferable action control from visual observations, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches the model to follow explicit task objectives. We train on tasks at different difficulty levels, from local operations and intermediate subgoals to complete objectives, with reasoning and memory summaries at key decision points. The need for reasoning is inherently sparse in long-horizon gameplay. Routine movement and repeated attacks favor direct action, while route failures, target switches, and resource decisions often require replanning. Gamer therefore uses single autoregressive policy to alternate between direct control, sparse reasoning, and memory updates. Persistent summaries carry task state across context boundaries. Figure 4 illustrates how adaptive reasoning and memory compaction are integrated into an interaction sequence. Figure 4 Sparse reasoning and cross-context memory in supervised fine-tuning. The shared autoregressive policy integrates visual observations, task memory, optional reasoning, and executable keyboard-mouse actions. Context memory compaction preserves task progress across long interactions, while adaptive reasoning allows the policy to act directly at routine steps and generate explicit reasoning when needed.

sections.title: 4 Temporal-Aware GRPO for Long-Horizon Policy Optimization
sections.content: CPT and SFT provide cross-game control and task-following capabilities, while online RL improves the policy on states encountered during its own interactions. Online RL in real-time games faces two challenges: long interactions can exceed the models context window, and delayed model responses can change the environment transitions observed during rollout collection. We address the first using Temporal-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO) and the second using the shared Streaming-vLLM infrastructure (Sec. 5). Together, they enable policy optimization over long sequences of real-time keyboard and mouse interaction. As illustrated in Figure 5, TA-GRPO divides long rollouts into finite segments linked by the same memory compaction mechanism used during SFT. It scores segments from separate rollouts of the same task using verifiable outcomes and assigns group-relative advantages [39] to the decisions within each segment. The policy can therefore learn from long interactions without fitting full trajectory into one context or repeatedly restoring an intermediate game state. The policy retains the same input and output format, generating reasoning, memory updates, and executable actions as needed.

sections.title: 5 Streaming-vLLM for Real-Time and Scalable Gameplay
sections.content: Real-time gameplay introduces timing constraints that are absent when evaluation pauses the game during inference. The results in Sec. 8.2 show that policy can perform well in paused game but degrade sharply when the game state changes before its actions arrive. This temporal mismatch also affects online policy optimization: delayed actions change subsequent states and the verified feedback in collected trajectories. At the same time, long-horizon training requires many independent environments to advance concurrently. 10 Practical gameplay and efficient online rollout collection therefore require low-latency serving that preserves state across turns. We develop Streaming-vLLM as common execution backend for training, evaluation, and deployment. The backend retains KV states across turns under memory compaction and reduces model execution cost. It also verifies structural tokens proposed by fast finite-state machine (FSM) and streams verified action blocks before the full packet is complete. The model-facing interface is shared across Qwen3-VL [3] and Qwen3.5 [36], including dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones. Architecture-specific kernels and schedules support each backbone while preserving the same observationaction protocol. Appendix reports representative Dense and MoE serving configurations on Ampere (NVIDIA A800) and Hopper (NVIDIA H200). Figure 6 Streaming-vLLM for persistent multi-environment inference. Each game client maintains separate short-term history, long-term memory, and logical KV-cache state. Paged allocation and memory-aware KV-cache reuse avoid repeated context processing, while incremental rotary position embedding (RoPE) refresh corrects retained keys after compaction. The runtime combines architecture-aware execution, BF16-verified FSM speculation, and early action dispatch to serve concurrent real-time interactions.

sections.title: 5.1 Memory-Compacted Streaming Context
sections.content: At each interaction step, the model consumes the control specification, task instruction, long-term memory, and recent observation-action history (B, I, Mt, Ht). Re-encoding the visual and textual history at every turn would repeat the same prefill work. As shown in Figure 6, Streaming-vLLM instead preserves KV states of retained context and computes new states only for newly appended tokens, following stateful streaming inference [53, 54]. short-term queue holds recent complete interaction rounds, while long-term queue stores generated memory summaries. At compaction boundary, the policy summarizes history before eviction. The discarded rounds release their KV pages, and recent rounds retain cached states. Each environment keeps its own logical-to-physical block table over the paged allocator [16], allowing requests with different history lengths to coexist. Compaction also changes the logical token positions of retained states. We update the rotary phase of the corresponding cached keys using the positional shift, without recomputing their projections or modifying the value cache. The retained cache preserves state across turns, so it need not be numerically equivalent to full re-encoding of the shortened context. The precise RoPE refresh and its scope are detailed in Appendix C.2. The same bounded history and persistent summaries are used in SFT and to link TA-GRPO trajectory segments.

sections.title: 5.2 Architecture-Aware Execution Across Backbones
sections.content: Frequent short requests incur costs beyond prefill, including decoder launches, inter-device communication, and architecture-specific operations. Streaming-vLLM separates common serving interface from specialized 11 execution paths. Dense and MoE variants share action serialization, context compaction, and client scheduling, while the compute backend accommodates their respective attention, expert, and recurrent or gated-deltanetwork operations. We combine operator fusion, tensor-parallel execution, communication overlap, and CUDA Graph replay to reduce serial overhead. We apply tensor parallelism selectively. It can reduce decoder compute time, but communication and synchronization may outweigh the savings for the smaller ViT workload. The measured tradeoff is analyzed in Table 9. On NVIDIA H200, C++ and bare-PTX BF16 backend further reduces kernel and orchestration costs on the critical path. Optional W8A8 paths are evaluated independently because lower precision does not always improve latency at given model size or tensor-parallel degree. We assess portability across model families and hardware configurations. We support Qwen3-VL [3] dense models at 2B, 4B, 8B, and 32B and its 30B-A3B MoE model, as well as Qwen3.5 [36] dense models at 0.8B, 2B, 9B, and 27B and its 35B-A3B MoE model. Our experiments and analysis cover representative Qwen3-VL Dense and Qwen3.5 MoE workloads across A800 and H200. The appendix compares numerical precision and tensor-parallel settings on each GPU.

sections.title: 5.3 Verified FSM Decoding and Streaming Actions
sections.content: After execution overhead is reduced, autoregressive generation remains sequential. fast finite-state-machine (FSM) drafter proposes predictable structural tokens in the reasoningaction output. The FSM tracks <think>, </think>, <action_start>, and <action_end> boundaries. It proposes closing an empty reasoning span or starting an action packet after reasoning ends. Within the action, it drafts whitespace after mouse-coordinate numbers, the separator following the coordinate, and predictable delimiters and empty-key patterns across the six keyboard-mouse groups. Mouse-coordinate values remain model-generated. The target model verifies FSM proposals using BF16 computation, and only accepted prefixes are committed. The policy retains control over action selection, while verification reduces the number of sequential decoding iterations. See Appendix C.1 for more details. Streaming-vLLM also reduces the time to the first executable action. Once the mouse fields and first verified key block are ready, the server sends that prefix to the client while the remaining blocks continue decoding. The client executes the six blocks in order, maintaining key press-hold-release semantics. Action execution can therefore begin while the remaining blocks are still being generated. The theoretical block-generation rate reported in the system ablation and the nominal 30 Hz client control protocol are distinct measurements, as clarified in Appendix C.4.

sections.title: 5.4 Concurrent Serving for Online Rollouts
sections.content: Real-time rollouts require scheduling that accounts for both action deadlines and throughput. Each game environment maintains its own short-term history, long-term memory, KV pages, and timing deadlines. shared scheduler batches context extension and decoding while limiting queueing delays that could make actions stale. This balances aggregate throughput against the progress rate of each active environment. Real-time evaluation and TA-GRPO training share the same serving path, so training rollouts are collected under the same execution protocol while the game continues to advance. Stateful cache reuse reduces the cost of long contexts, architecture-specific backends support different models and GPUs, and verified FSM drafting reduces action-generation cost. Combined with early action dispatch, these components enable responsive, high-frequency control and parallel RL rollouts linked by memory summaries. Section 8.6 reports latency and closed-loop evaluations, and Appendix C.4 provides representative GPU, precision, and parallelism settings.

sections.title: 6 Data Construction for Cross-Game Learning
sections.content: Raw gameplay videos provide rich visual and control experience, but they rarely specify the players objective, the decisions that require reasoning, or the information that should be retained beyond the recent context. We develop scalable annotation pipeline that turns heterogeneous recordings into supervision for long-horizon task following, as shown in Figure 7. Starting from tens of thousands of hours of raw gameplay collected across different sources, we filter invalid or misaligned recordings and balance coverage across gameplay 12 scenarios. For SFT, we curate approximately 1K hours of gameplay trajectories. GPT-5.6-Luna [30] generates sparse action reasoning, task segments with instructions and scene descriptions, and task-state memories. We organize these annotations into three instruction levels: local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages. Figure 7 Bottom-up construction of multi-level task supervision. The diagram illustrates the organization of aligned gameplay segments into local operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages. Separate GPT-5.6-Luna passes produce sparse Think annotations, segment-level instructions and scene descriptions, and memory updates as detailed in Secs. 6.2-6.3. The diagram focuses on hierarchy assembly rather than depicting every annotation call.

sections.title:
6.1 Trajectory Preparation and Temporal Alignment
Data sources, filtering, and scenario balancing. We collect raw gameplay recordings with associated keyboard
and mouse events from multiple sources. Within this collection, the HSR recording track contains roughly 68K
sessions and 11K hours of video. Rather than annotating all available videos, we first select recordings with
reliable visual and action supervision. We reject corrupted or duplicated sessions, missing or discontinuous
frames, and trajectories whose video and action timestamps cannot be aligned consistently. We also remove
invalid action traces, including mouse coordinates outside the valid screen or control bounds, malformed action
states, and events that cross recording or interaction boundaries. Long inactive periods and recordings without
meaningful interaction are filtered, while valid held inputs and task-related waiting periods are retained.
sections.content: Filtering alone would leave the instruction corpus dominated by frequently recorded activities. We therefore balance scenario coverage by limiting repeated behaviors and retaining less frequent interactions and longer task transitions. After these quality and coverage checks, we obtain approximately 3.2K sessions and 1K hours of video, which we use as the source for SFT annotation. Action-observation alignment. We retain the original ordering of keyboard and mouse events and associate each action block with its corresponding frame using corrected recording timestamps. Each device-level action interval spans approximately 200 ms and contains the six finer control blocks defined in Sec. 2.1. Source videos are sampled to obtain the visual observations used for annotation. When frame indices are discontinuous, or timestamps show recording gap, an action window is not allowed to cross that boundary. Short button presses are kept as short pulses rather than being dropped by temporal aggregation. This preserves movement duration and interaction timing while producing the same executable action interface used by the policy.

sections.title: 6.2 Sparse Reasoning and Visual Task Segmentation
sections.content: The annotation process separates local action reasoning from longer visual task understanding. Short videoaction windows identify key decisions, while longer visual clips reveal task structure and progress. We use GPT-5.6-Luna for both annotation passes and align their outputs by the original frame IDs and recording timestamps. Decision-focused Thinking. We divide the action stream into windows of 50 device-level action intervals, 13 corresponding to roughly 10 seconds of interaction. Each window contains 25 ordered game observations and the associated 50 action intervals. GPT-5.6-Luna identifies sparse set of decision points, typically when the player selects or corrects route, handles new interaction prompt, changes objective, recovers from an unsuccessful attempt, or responds to significant scene transition. Each Think annotation describes the observed outcome, the current decision, and an intended next action. Continuous movement, repeated controls, and minor camera corrections usually receive no separate reasoning target. Windows with neither meaningful input nor visual change can be skipped. This process yields approximately 1.2M timestamp-aligned Think annotations. Long-context instruction and scene annotation. We divide each session into the minimum number of equallength visual clips of at most 288 seconds. Frames are selected at approximately one-second intervals and arranged into 3 2 timestamped mosaics, yielding at most 49 mosaic images per clip. This lets GPT-5.6-Luna inspect continuous visual context without exceeding the image-input budget. The model identifies contiguous task segments and assigns each task instruction, gameplay label, and short scene description of the visible evidence. These task segments provide the temporal and semantic basis for the instruction hierarchy. We prompt the model to segment gameplay by the players current task. Brief movements and reward collection are grouped with the task they support, while an explicit challenge restart begins new segment. Postprocessing adjusts adjacent segment boundaries to form continuous timeline and converts clip-relative start and end times to timestamps in the original recording. This yields approximately 63K task segments, with median duration of about 40 seconds. The activity labels cover seven gameplay categories: navigation, NPC dialogue, combat, minigames, system menus, Currency Wars, and other activities.

sections.title: 6.3 Memory Annotation from Continuous Visual Context
sections.content: After task segmentation, we reuse the clip images and cleaned task segments in second conversational turn to generate memory annotations. The model returns all summaries for the clip in one response, typically one per 16-second window. Each summary briefly describes, in the first person, the cumulative accomplishments and outcomes within the clip up to the window end. final window shorter than 8 seconds is merged into the preceding window. Postprocessing associates each summary with the active task instruction and the latest image frame at or before the window end. The dataset contains approximately 223K memory annotations. At each training step, we condition the policy on the latest summary whose end timestamp is no later than the current observation. The annotation model receives the complete visual clip and is prompted to summarize only events up to each window end.

sections.title:
6.4 Three-Level Instruction Construction
Building on the first-pass task segments, we construct easy, medium, and hard instructions according to
the scope of the objective and the number of annotated decisions it covers. These levels correspond to local
operations, intermediate subgoals, and extended task stages, respectively. The same recorded interval can
support instructions at multiple levels.
sections.content: Easy: local operations. Easy instructions cover one or two annotated decisions, such as approaching an NPC, selecting menu option, or collecting an item. Medium: intermediate subgoals. Medium instructions combine related operations into subgoal spanning three to five annotated decisions, such as navigating around an obstruction and completing the required interaction. Hard: extended task stages. Hard instructions connect multiple subgoals into task stage spanning six or more annotated decisions, such as navigating through several areas and resolving intervening challenges. We construct the instruction hierarchy bottom-up from temporally aligned annotations. Task-segment instructions and scene descriptions establish the activity and its boundaries, Think annotations identify key decisions, and memories track task progress. We group adjacent operations that advance common subgoal, then combine related subgoals into extended task stages. Human-annotated examples guide the wording and scope of the generated instructions. sections.title: 7.1 Model and Training Configuration
sections.content: Gamer supports both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures across Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.5 families. The trained models share the same autoregressive keyboard-mouse action interface without an additional output head. We first analyze CPT scaling across 120 controlled Qwen3.5 Dense configurations, referred to as GameScaling. Guided by these findings, we train Gamer from Qwen3-VL-8B with additional HSR gameplay data. Training follows three stages while preserving the model architecture and action representation. CPT learns transferable control with key remapping and repeat-aware loss decay. SFT introduces multi-level task supervision, sparse reasoning, and cross-context memory. TA-GRPO then improves long-horizon behavior through online interaction, using environment-verifiable rewards and temporal credit assignment. Gameplay trajectories are sampled at 5 Hz, with six action blocks per step providing approximately 30 Hz control and local visual history of 20 frames. We extend Verl [40] into unified training and evaluation framework, using Streaming-vLLM for interactive evaluation and online RL rollouts. sharded inference service pool backed by 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs serves 32 parallel game environments. Each RL iteration collects 128 rollouts in groups of 8, with environment-verifiable rewards and no learned process reward model. Updated policy weights are synchronized across the service pool before the next rollout collection, keeping policy versions aligned throughout online training. sections.title: 7.2 Data Composition and Sampling
sections.content: Our training data combines cross-game interaction trajectories, general multimodal data, multi-level task supervision, and online policy experience. Figure 8 summarizes how these sources are filtered and routed into the CPT, SFT, and RL stages, while Table 2 reports their corresponding usage and scale. In the CPT stage, we perform controlled scaling experiments (i.e., GameScaling) using mixture of VPT [4], D2E [8], and OpenP2P [56] gameplay data while holding the token ratio at 85% gameplay and 15% general vision-language data (Appendix B.1). General multimodal data sources include LLaVA-OneVision [19], Zebra-CoT [18], GameQA [42], Embodied-Reasoner [62], and Cambrian-S [55]. Gamers CPT stage retains this data mixture ratio and adds additional HSR gameplay trajectories. In the SFT stage, we annotate approximately 1K hours of curated HSR gameplay trajectories. As described in Sec. 6.4, operation-level examples train local control and sparse reasoning. Subgoal-level examples add intermediate objectives and longer memory, while task-level examples cover complete long-horizon tasks. Examples at different annotation levels may come from the same trajectory and we count their derived samples and supervision tokens separately. To improve coverage across gameplay scenarios, we downsample overrepresented streams and excessively idle intervals while preserving meaningful movement, held controls, and waiting periods. In the HSR portion of the CPT corpus, filtering retains approximately 149K aligned clips, corresponding to around 332 hours of gameplay. Data splits are assigned at the recording or complete-task level before creating overlapping windows or multi-level examples, so derived samples from source remain in the same split.

sections.title:
7.3 Automated RL Environment
A shared infrastructure for learning, evaluation, and testing. Many existing game-RL benchmarks run as
lightweight, self-contained simulators that can be reset cheaply and queried directly for rewards. Modern
commercial games present a substantially harder setting. In particular, Honkai: Star Rail depends on a full
game client, supporting online services, GPU-accelerated rendering, and complex game-state dependencies.
Reproducing its native mechanics in a lightweight simulator would change the interaction setting, while simply
replicating game clients does not provide controlled initialization or objective verification. These challenges
extend beyond online RL to large-scale automated evaluation and gameplay testing, where hundreds of
executions must start from comparable states and be judged against consistent success criteria. We therefore
sections.content: 16 build dedicated, engine-instrumented sandbox that makes this resource-intensive game reproducible, verifiable, and scalable without changing the agents visual-control interface. Game-native rules as unified source of feedback. We adapt the game engine to expose task-relevant state transitions and completion conditions to the environment backend. The resulting rule-based verifiers serve three complementary purposes. During online RL, they provide environment-verifiable rewards for TA-GRPO without learned process reward model. During evaluation, they measure task completion objectively across models and policy checkpoints. For automated gameplay testing, the same checks provide reproducible pass/fail criteria for interactions and quest progression. This shared verification layer avoids relying on subjective assessments of generated text or inferring complex task outcomes from individual screenshots. GM-controlled initialization and reproducible execution. We integrate game-master (GM) commands to prepare predefined task states and restore the corresponding conditions before an episode. Each task pairs an initialization procedure with target state, completion check, and termination rule. This allows the same objective to be executed repeatedly for policy optimization, fair comparison, and systematic testing of game behaviors. It also makes failed executions easier to reproduce and inspect. Crucially, all privileged engine access remains within the environment backend. The policy receives only screen observations and task context, and its actions are executed through the same keyboardmouse interface used in real gameplay. Scalable execution across use cases. We construct verifiable environments spanning navigation, dialogue and interaction, and game-specific puzzle mechanics. For online RL, 32 parallel Windows game environments are served by sharded Streaming-vLLM inference pool backed by 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each iteration collects 128 trajectories in groups of eight, with policy checkpoints synchronized before the next collection round. The same initialization, execution, and verification interfaces also support batched evaluation and automated regression tests without manually resetting or judging each attempt. Beyond enabling real-time policy optimization, this infrastructure provides practical foundation for scalable assessment and testing in modern commercial games. Sec. 8.1 introduces the held-out side-quest and minigame evaluations.

sections.title: 8 Experiments
sections.content: Our evaluation examines three complementary questions. First, we summarize the study in GameScaling, which evaluates 120 CPT configurations to characterize the effects of model scale, gameplay budget, and data composition. We then assess the executable cross-game performance of CPT policies built on Dense and MoE backbones. Next, we evaluate the separately trained HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT and its SFT and RL successors on HSR side quests and minigames, separating broad interaction skills from long-horizon task execution. Finally, we test whether real-time rollout collection supports online learning and whether Streaming-vLLM delivers the accuracy and latency needed for sustained interaction. All interactive evaluations use the shared keyboard-mouse interface.

sections.title:
8.1 Evaluation Setup
Public game benchmarks. We evaluate game-control policies on MCU [63], ViZDoom [52], OmniGameArena [23],
and GameWorld [32]. These benchmarks vary in how far they differ from the gameplay data used for CPT.
Specifically, MCU and ViZDoom evaluate game domains represented during CPT and primarily measure
control learning within training-covered environments. OmniGameArena evaluates transfer to unseen three-
dimensional games with related interaction semantics. GameWorld provides a more distant cross-game transfer
setting with larger shifts in visual appearance, control mechanics, and task structure.
sections.content: We follow the task definitions, environment settings, and native scoring protocols of the corresponding benchmarks. Each benchmark retains its original evaluation metric. We distinguish idealized time-paused (TP) evaluation from real-time (RT) interaction. TP pauses the environment during model inference, whereas RT allows the game to continue advancing. In the public game comparison, we report the RT score as the main value and its signed difference from TP (RTTP) in parentheses. Across game evaluations, we use the same set of strong multimodal baselines wherever they support the required visual-control interface. These include GPT-6.1-Sol [31], Gemini-3.8-Flash [12], GPT-5.6-Sol [30], 17 GPT-5.6-Luna [30], Claude-Opus-5.0 [1], GLM-5.3-Flash [57], and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision [9]. The same baseline pool is reused in the Honkai: Star Rail side-quest and minigame evaluations to provide consistent comparison across control, instruction following, and gameplay generalization. Honkai: Star Rail evaluation suite. We construct two complementary evaluation sets in Honkai: Star Rail, comprising side quests and minigame tasks held out from training (Figure 9). Although the final CPT model has seen other gameplay from the same game, it has not been trained on these evaluation tasks or their target completions. This setting tests generalization to new tasks within familiar game, rather than zero-shot transfer to an unseen game. The first set contains two long-horizon side quests that test sustained progress on complex instructions. Each quest may combine navigation, dialogue, combat, puzzles, and item interactions across several intermediate objectives. To finish quest, the agent must remember quest information, track subgoal progress, and use that task state to guide low-level control. The two evaluated quests are Opportunity Makes the Thief (Part I) and Bestial Ferocity. They contain 30 and 55 evaluation milestones, grouped into 22 and 40 parent steps, respectively. The first quest combines navigation, dialogue, combat, and UI interaction. The second also includes three automaton-repair puzzles and repeated visits to earlier locations. The total time budgets across milestones are 30 minutes and 100 minutes, respectively. Each quest has fixed initial state, task objective, milestone sequence, verifier, and termination condition. We report accuracy as the fraction of evaluated task executions that succeed, both overall and for each interaction type. The milestone inventory covers navigation, dialogue, combat, UI interaction, and, where applicable, puzzle solving. These rates measure verified progress across task executions rather than uninterrupted end-to-end quest completion. The complete milestones, types, and budgets are given in Appendix D. The second subset contains 40 instances across 7 minigame types, covering pattern composition, logical reasoning, spatial reasoning, temporal planning, and timing-sensitive control. Each type contains between one and sixteen evaluated instances. Figure 10 illustrates the minigame mechanics and instance distribution. We report the success rates for each type and compute overall accuracy as the unweighted mean of the seven type-level rates. Each type therefore contributes equally, regardless of its number of instances. Per-instance evaluation and taxonomy are described in Appendix D.

sections.title: 8.4 Instruction Generalization across Diverse Minigames
sections.content: The minigame suite emphasizes instruction following across different gameplay mechanics. This broader coverage is important because the tasks require different combinations of spatial reasoning, rule interpretation, visual matching, and device-level interaction rather than single repeated control routine. Table 7 reports success for each of the seven types and their unweighted macro-average. Instruction tuning broadens success across distinct minigame mechanics. The seven-type macro-average increases from 3.2% for the base Qwen3-VL-8B to 15.0% for Gamer-CPT and 39.2% for Gamer-SFT, further gain of 24.2 percentage points after instruction tuning. SFT reaches 76.2% on Januss Hidden Passage, 52.4% on Januss Maze, and 50.0% on Navigation Compass. It also obtains non-zero mean success in all seven types, compared with three for the base model. The CPT checkpoint already improves the macro-average, providing useful foundation for responding to gameplay observations and actions. SFT then connects these control capabilities to task-specific goals, which is reflected in improvements across puzzles with different interfaces and completion rules. The evaluation tasks are held out from training, so the comparison measures generalization to new instances and objectives within HSR. Online RL further improves performance across diverse mechanics. Following SFT, Gamer-RL raises the 23 seven-type macro-average from 39.2% to 49.7%, an additional gain of 10.5 percentage points. The improvement is particularly pronounced on Navigation Compass, where accuracy increases from 50.0% to 95.8%. RL also improves Magflow Link from 40.0% to 53.3%, Hexanexus from 11.1% to 33.3% and Januss Hidden Passage from 76.2% to 81.0%, with additional gains on Abacus Circuitry and Golden Scapegoat. These results extend the benefits of online policy optimization beyond long-horizon quests to tasks involving diverse rules and interaction patterns. Together, the CPT, SFT, and RL stages progressively improve the models ability to interpret instructions and execute actions across different game mechanics. To prevent game types with more tasks from dominating the aggregate, the overall metric first averages attempts within each task and then gives each of the seven types equal weight. This makes the reported improvement measure of breadth across mechanics rather than only the most frequent minigame.

8.5 Impact of Real-Time Rollouts on Online RL
Real-time interaction is critical for online RL in modern games. Unlike lightweight simulators, modern games
involve continuously evolving environments, complex gameplay mechanics, and state-dependent interactions.
In this setting, inference latency affects not only the responsiveness of the deployed agent but also the quality
and efficiency of online policy learning. Delayed control can cause subsequent actions to operate on outdated
observations, making it harder to obtain timely feedback from the environment. We therefore examine the
effect of rollout frequency on RL training, comparing real-time Streaming-vLLM against standard vLLM
rollouts. The game continues to advance under both settings.

sections.title: 8.6 Streaming-vLLM
sections.content: In addition to low latency, an inference engine must preserve the models ability Streaming video benchmarks. to understand and respond to continuously arriving visual input. To verify the inference accuracy of our StreamingVLLM, we further evaluate streaming inference on StreamingBench [22] and OVO-Bench [29]. For StreamingBench, we use the Real-Time Visual Understanding subset. OVO-Bench evaluates current-event understanding through Real, retrieval of earlier information through Backward, and delayed response after sufficient evidence through Forward. We first test whether stateful streaming preserves online visual understanding. The controlled comparison uses the same backbone checkpoint, hardware, numerical precision, decoding configuration, and cache budget across inference methods. We compare Streaming-vLLM against DSCache [34], InfiniPot-V [15], and uniform streaming-cache baseline corresponding to the caching strategy used by StreamingVLM [54]. The evaluation reports StreamingBench Real-Time accuracy, OVO-Bench Overall and its Real, Backward, and Forward subsets, query latency, and peak GPU memory. Streaming-vLLM preserves visual understanding while reducing inference latency. Table 8 presents matchedbackbone comparisons on two complementary streaming benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-8B, Streaming-vLLM scores 83.29 on StreamingBench and 62.3 on OVO-Bench, reducing query latency from 0.53 to 0.08 relative to DSCache. With Qwen3.5-9B, it reaches 83.77 and 60.9, respectively, while latency falls from 1.56 to 0.16 s. The OVO-Bench improvements appear in its Real, Backward, and Forward subsets, suggesting that the retained context remains useful for both incoming visual evidence and information from earlier video frames. The results are particularly relevant to interactive agents, as reducing latency is only useful if the system can still interpret the observations needed for its next decision. These comparisons show that the serving optimizations do not require sacrificing the measured streaming-video accuracy on either backbone. End-to-end performance depends on optimizing the full interaction path. Table 9 traces successive runtime configurations for the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE model on H200. The initial TP4 streaming configuration offers only modest change in total latency relative to the TP1 baseline. Vision processing, prefill, and autoregressive decoding impose different computational and communication costs, so accelerating one component does not necessarily reduce the complete request time by the same proportion. This motivates the use of architectureaware kernels and overlapping execution rather than relying on tensor parallelism alone. Because some configurations also change profiling boundaries, the table reports cumulative system improvements rather than isolated single-factor effects. Cumulative runtime optimizations yield substantial latency reduction. Operator fusion, parallel overlap, CUDA Graph replay, and the low-overhead megakernel backend progressively reduce request latency. FSMguided drafting further shortens action generation, while BF16 target-model verification preserves the target policys acceptance decision. Together, these cumulative optimizations reduce end-to-end latency from approximately 1.31 to 65 ms, which is 20.1 speedup on the measured H200 MoE configuration. The latency reduction also increases the capacity to produce executable action packets within fixed wall-clock interval. These are throughput-derived capacities, not direct measurements of the clients realized game frame rate, which follows its own execution schedule. This distinction allows the system results to quantify available inference headroom without conflating request throughput with observed gameplay cadence.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: Gamer learns to control diverse and complex games through shared keyboard-and-mouse interface. It combines large-scale continued pre-training, task-conditioned supervised fine-tuning, and temporal-aware reinforcement learning to learn transferable control, long-horizon reasoning, and persistent memory. StreamingvLLM supports both training and deployment, enabling real-time interaction and efficient online rollouts while reducing latency-induced bias in reinforcement learning. At inference time, Gamer acts through visual observations and device-level controls without privileged game state or game-engine modifications. Environment-side task verification is used separately to provide online RL rewards. These capabilities could effectively reduce development costs through automated testing, faster game iteration, and new gameplay mechanics. By supporting real-time interaction without game-specific infrastructure, Gamer offers basis for agents that learn and improve across complex 3D games and other interactive environments.

sections.title: 10 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Several main directions remain for extending Gamers scope and accessibility. First, our evaluation covers selected set of environments and task structures. The shared observation-action interface provides basis for extending joint post-training and systematic evaluation to broader interactive settings. Our preliminary results suggest the potential for improving performance and generalization by scaling relevant gameplay data across broader range of environments. These benefits depend on the coverage and composition of the training experience. Second, Streaming-vLLM enables real-time interaction on the evaluated GPU platforms, while further reductions in serving costs would support wider deployment. Model compression and additional runtime optimizations offer promising directions for extending this efficiency to more resource-constrained settings while preserving responsiveness and task performance. Third, although Gamer improves the trade-off between response latency and task performance in the evaluated settings, reasoning capability may remain bottleneck in environments that demand deeper deliberation. Fast, continuous interaction alone does not ensure the ability to solve complex strategic problems. Our framework provides foundation for exploring hierarchical game agents that combine larger model for deliberative System 2 reasoning with fast model for reactive System 1 execution. Such architectures could coordinate longer-term planning with timely control, extending the range of tasks that agents can handle under real-time constraints.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Generalist Game Agents Research on game-playing agents has expanded from environment-specific policies to general models combining perception, reasoning, memory, and executable control. Large-scale behavioral pretraining provides one route: VPT [4] learns Minecraft control from internet videos labeled by an inverse dynamics model, while STEVE-1 [21] extends this paradigm to language-conditioned behavior. Other systems, including DEPS [48], Voyager [44], JARVIS-1 [50], Optimus-1 [20], and OmniJARVIS [49], incorporate planning, reusable skills, and memory to support increasingly complex tasks. Recent work further targets generalization across tasks and worlds. Gato [38] and SIMA [37] study shared policies across heterogeneous environments, while Game-TARS [51] and Lumine [41] combine reasoning, memory, and native keyboardmouse control for extended gameplay. NitroGen [26] and OpenP2P [56] instead emphasize scalable visual policy learning from broad gameplay data. These approaches address different aspects of generalist gameplay, typically emphasizing cross-environment reactive control or extended reasoning under more specialized training settings. We combine cross-game continued pre-training with task-oriented policy optimization for sustained interaction. A.2 Scalable Gameplay Learning Progress in game agents increasingly relies on large and heterogeneous interaction data. MineRL [14] and MineDojo [11] provide structured demonstrations and multimodal resources, while VPT [4] scales behavioral learning through inverse dynamics. D2E [8], NitroGen [26], and OpenP2P [56] broaden supervision through desktop trajectories, visible control overlays, and inverse-dynamics-labeled gameplay. GameHorizon [47] further introduces multi-level annotations spanning operations, subgoals, and strategies. Transfer also depends on model size and data composition. General scaling and continual-pretraining studies show that performance depends jointly on model capacity, data budget, and domain mixture. In gameplay, VPT [4] demonstrates the value of large-scale behavioral pretraining, while OpenP2P [56] studies scaling through both predictive performance and causal behavior. GameScaling varies model size, interaction budget, and game composition to distinguish between gains obtained by learning shared control interface and gains that depend on target-relevant gameplay. Scale alone is not sufficient for task-oriented gameplay. Effective policy learning also requires supervision that connects local actions with higher-level objectives. GameHorizon [47] introduces temporal hierarchy into gameplay supervision, while OmniJARVIS [49] and Lumine [41] combine reasoning, memory, and staged training. We train the policy with supervision at the operation, subgoal, and task levels, and retain compact task summaries across context boundaries. A.3 Memory and Long-Horizon Interaction Sustained gameplay also requires agents to retain task-relevant information after earlier interactions leave the active context. Existing agents address this through reusable skills, retrieved experience, or compressed interaction histories. Voyager stores executable skills, JARVIS-1 [50] and Optimus-1 [20] retrieve accumulated experience, and Game-TARS [51] combines recent interactions with compressed textual history. OmniJARVIS [49] and Lumine [41] further integrate memory with reasoning and action generation. We explicitly supervise task summaries and use them as persistent task state during supervised training, online policy optimization, and streaming inference. Feedback-based optimization provides complementary mechanism for improving extended behavior. GRPO [39] optimizes relative advantages across groups of sampled outputs, while GUI-R1 [24] and Game-RL [42] adapt reinforcement learning to executable GUI actions and multimodal game reasoning. Game-TARS [51] also refines thoughtaction trajectories through action-consistency-based filtering. We optimize finite trajectory segments linked by compressed memory, updating task-state maintenance and executable behavior together. Long-horizon interaction must also operate under bounded context and latency. StreamingLLM [53] maintains stable inference with fixed attention window, while InfiniPot-V [15], DSCache [34], and StreamingVLM [54] explore compressed or structured memory for continuous visual streams. Serving techniques such as PagedAttention [16] and speculative decoding further reduce autoregressive inference cost. S1 uses Minecraft exclusively. S2-S4 draw from the same 80 canonical game labels with different sampling weights, and S5 removes Minecraft, leaving 79 labels. You can find more details in Table 10. Consequently, the five mixtures should not be interpreted as monotonic increase in the number of game worlds. We summarize diversity using the effective number of worlds, exp( (cid:80) pw log pw), which accounts for the balance of gameplay samples across game labels. The fixed non-Minecraft pool contains 124 source-stream labels mapping to 79 canonical game labels. The three validation distributions separate Minecraft held-out clips, training-covered game clips, and title-disjoint unseen-game clips. The latter is game-balanced, with 28 unseen titles and 160 clips per title (4,480 clips in total). Grouping by source recording and removing title aliases limit overlap between training and validation. sections.title: F Training Recipe and Reproducibility Details
sections.content: F.1 Unified Verl-Based Training and Inference We extend Verl [40] to use shared game-interaction interface across CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO. The training framework handles the stage-specific objectives and model updates, while Streaming-vLLM supplies autoregressive policy inference for interactive evaluation and online RL rollouts. The stages share the keyboard-mouse action grammar, observation-action history representation, and game-facing execution interface. CPT and SFT learn from recorded trajectories under their respective objectives, and TA-GRPO receives environment-verifiable feedback from interactions generated by the current policy. Consequently, the final policy is evaluated through the same type of executable control path used to collect online training experience. Consistency scope. The system keeps action serialization, token boundaries, and environment timing consistent between training-stage evaluation and online policy interaction. It does not imply that every forward pass uses the same numerical kernel or cached context. Training computes gradients on supervised or rollout-derived sequences, whereas Streaming-vLLM uses stateful KV reuse, memory compaction, and architecture-dependent serving kernels. The RoPE phase adjustment in Appendix C.2 corrects retained cache positions but does not reconstruct the output of fully re-encoded context. Consistency therefore refers to the policy interface and 50 interaction semantics, not bitwise equality of training and inference logits. F.2 Training Configuration and Data Separation Controlled CPT configurations. The scaling study consists of four backbone sizes, five game mixtures, and six completed training budgets. It uses twenty primary Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) trunks, one per size-mixture pair. The shorter-budget checkpoints branch from their shared trunk and complete an independent decay phase within the stated total budget, yielding 120 evaluated configurations. All controlled runs use an 85% gameplay and 15% general vision-language token ratio, which is also retained for the separately trained HSR-augmented Gamer-CPT checkpoint. The CPT recipe uses BF16 AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0, and peak learning rates of 105 for the language model and 7 106 for the unfrozen vision encoder. The WSD allocation is 3% warmup, 87.3% stable training, and 9.7% cosine decay. The controlled grid uses 854480 observations, twenty visual turns per context, and approximately 2.3 105 supervised target tokens per update. Cross-stage implementation. The same autoregressive device-level action representation is retained in CPT, SFT, and TA-GRPO, while instruction and memory conditioning are added in the later stages. The full stage-by-stage recipe, including the image resolution actually configured for each stage, is summarized in Table 15. For the real-time RL stage, the rollout-worker and training configuration are recorded separately from the controlled CPT grid. The short-term history uses 20 dialogue turns, the memory budget is 512 tokens, and each TA-GRPO segment is bounded by 20 dialogue turns with temporal factor β = 0.9. Evaluation separation. Training/validation/test splits are defined at the complete recording or task-source level before extracting overlapping action windows or multi-level examples. For interaction benchmarks, time-paused (TP) evaluation freezes the simulated environment during policy inference, whereas real-time (RT) evaluation lets the environment advance. These settings use the same action serialization but different timing semantics. Real-time performance comparisons should therefore report both the serving configuration and environment timing rather than treating model size or score as proxy for latency. F.3 Execution Protocol and Reproducibility Rollout and evaluation protocol. Interactive inference produces six keyboard-mouse control blocks from the current visual observation, task instruction, and memory context. The client executes these blocks while the environment continues to advance. Online RL runs across 32 parallel game environments served by sharded Streaming-vLLM pool with 64 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each iteration gathers 128 rollouts in groups of eight from the active navigation or puzzle task pool. Two disjoint rollout subsets support the policy updates, and environment task verification provides rewards without learned process reward model. SFT and RL evaluations use matched task initializations, milestone verifiers, action semantics, and inference settings as described in Sec. 8.3. Reproducibility boundary. After the two policy updates, the resulting checkpoint is synchronized across the inference services, and the next rollout iteration starts only after the workers acknowledge the expected policy version. Our run audit records the trainer and inference revisions, checkpoints, action serialization, tokenizer, image preprocessing, and environment settings. Inference uses BF16 with maximum generation length of 512 tokens and temperature 0.9. The game screenshots are captured at 1280 720 and resized to 854 480 for model input. TA-GRPO uses 20-turn segments and temporal factor β = 0.9.
